PRIVATE SCHOOL TUITION DISCOUNT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What does your sticker price really collect? Discount rate and net tuition

Enter your sticker tuition and the students in each financial-aid group. The tool shows your discount rate, net tuition per student and break-even enrollment, whether a student with a given award still adds money, and what a tuition increase really brings in when aid is held flat or grows with the price.

The method with a worked example: tuition discount rate explained.

1. The school

2. Students by financial-aid group

One row per group of similar awards. Full-pay families are a group with an award of zero. Up to eight.

How it is built

Net tuition: students times sticker price, less the average award of each group times its students. The discount rate is total aid divided by gross tuition.

Break-even enrollment: fixed costs divided by what each student adds after their extra cost, at your current aid mix. Highest useful award: sticker price minus the extra cost of a student; below it, one more student adds money.

Increases: each scenario raises the sticker price and either holds every award at today's dollars or scales awards with the price, then removes the share of families you expect to lose. The test suite checks that these figures tie to the plain arithmetic.

Common questions

What is a tuition discount rate?

It is financial aid given as a share of gross tuition: total aid divided by sticker tuition times the number of students. A school with a $24,000 sticker price and $2,120,000 of aid across 300 students has a discount rate of 29.4%. It is a measure of how much of the sticker price the school actually collects.

How do I calculate net tuition revenue?

Multiply sticker tuition by the number of students to get gross tuition, then subtract the aid awarded to every student. What remains is net tuition revenue. Divide by the number of students for net tuition per student.

Should a school raise tuition or hold aid flat?

If aid stays the same in dollars, every dollar of a sticker increase on a paying family is kept and the discount rate falls. If aid grows with the sticker price, the discount rate stays the same and less of the increase is kept. The tool shows both side by side, with the number of families you expect to lose to the higher price.

Does an extra student with financial aid still help the budget?

Yes, while the award is smaller than the sticker price minus the extra cost of that student, because fixed costs are paid either way. A seat that stays empty brings in nothing. The tool shows the highest award that still adds money.

Is my school's data uploaded?

No. Everything is calculated in your browser, there are no accounts, and nothing is sent to a server. Use Save to download a scenario file.

Is this financial or enrollment advice?

No. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Families react to price in ways a single number cannot predict, and aid decisions carry fairness and mission questions. Talk to your head of school, board finance committee or auditor.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type, not financial, accounting, legal or enrollment advice. Use at your own risk. Families respond to price and aid in ways a model cannot predict; check any decision with your head of school, board finance committee or auditor.

Independent. Not affiliated with any school association, accreditor, financial-aid assessment service or tuition-management company, and none is named or ranked here.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or backups of anything you enter.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (scenario_run, example_loaded, text_copied, csv_downloaded, file_saved) are counted in this browser only, and you can switch that off below.

Related tools: the childcare center break-even calculator and the childcare tuition calculator.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional.

Tuition discount rate: what the sticker price really collects

The sticker price is what the brochure says. Net tuition is what reaches the bank after financial aid. The share given away is the discount rate, and it moves the budget more than most line items.

The worked example

A school has 300 students and a $24,000 sticker price. 130 families pay in full. 60 receive an average $6,000, 50 receive $12,000, 40 receive $18,000 and 20 receive $22,000. Fixed costs are $4,300,000 a year and each extra student costs about $2,500.

Gross tuition is $7,200,000. Aid totals $2,120,000, so net tuition is $5,080,000 and the discount rate is 29.4%. Net per student is $16,933, which is the same money as 212 full-pay students.

After per-student costs and fixed costs the school is left with $30,000. At this aid mix it needs 298 students to break even, with 320 seats.

Raising the price: held aid or growing aid

If awards stay the same in dollars, a higher sticker price adds its full amount on every student and the discount rate falls. If awards rise in step with the price, the discount rate stays put and the school keeps less. With 0.2% of students leaving for every 1% of increase:

IncreaseSurplus, aid heldDiscount rateSurplus, aid growsDiscount rate
+4%$281,05628.3%$196,93429.4%
+6%$404,85627.8%$279,18229.4%

Holding awards flat is not free of consequence: it asks aided families to absorb the whole increase, which may cost the school the very students the aid exists for. The numbers show the trade; they do not decide it.

Does one more aided student pay?

While a student's award is below sticker price minus the extra cost they bring (here $21,500), they add money to a school that would otherwise leave the seat empty, because fixed costs are paid either way. Three of the four aided groups clear that bar. The near-full-aid group, at $22,000, sits $500 a student above it: each of those students costs the school slightly more than they pay, which is a mission decision the discount rate alone will not show.

If aid grows with the sticker price, the discount rate stays the same and less of the increase is kept.
